vulnerabilities.title: SECCOMP_SANDBOX_BYPASS_FD_REUSE

root_cause.description: The seccomp sandbox in setup_seccomp() constrains read() to fd==0 (stdin) and write() to fd==1 (stdout) using SCMP_CMP_EQ argument constraints. However, close(3), open(2), and openat(0x101) are all whitelisted with NO argument constraints. This allows an attacker to manipulate file descriptor allocation: close(0) frees fd 0, then open("/target_file") reuses fd 0 for the newly opened file. After this fd reuse, read(0, buf, n) reads from the opened file instead of stdin, bypassing the fd==0 constraint. Similarly, close(1) + open() reuses fd 1, allowing write(1, buf, n) to write to an arbitrary file. The sandbox's intended protection (preventing file content exfiltration by restricting read to stdin and write to stdout) is defeated because the fd number constraints are not bound to the original stdin/stdout file objects — they only check the integer fd value, which can be reassigned via close+open.

affected_objects: seccomp BPF rules for read(syscall=0) and write(syscall=1)

attack_surface.input: User-supplied shellcode (up to 4095 bytes) read into RWX mmap page and executed via call rax
data_flow: main() calls init() which calls setup_seccomp() to install seccomp sandbox before shellcode execution
setup_seccomp() at 0x11c5: seccomp_init(0) creates default-KILL filter context
Rule for write(syscall=1) at 0x1231: seccomp_rule_add(ctx, ALLOW, 1, 1, {arg=0, op=SCMP_CMP_EQ(4), datum_a=1, datum_b=0}) — write allowed only when fd==1
Rule for open(syscall=2) at 0x1258: seccomp_rule_add(ctx, ALLOW, 2, 0) — open allowed unconditionally
Rule for openat(syscall=0x101) at 0x127b: seccomp_rule_add(ctx, ALLOW, 0x101, 0) — openat allowed unconditionally
Rule for close(syscall=3) at 0x129e: seccomp_rule_add(ctx, ALLOW, 3, 0) — close allowed unconditionally
Rule for read(syscall=0) at 0x12ed: seccomp_rule_add(ctx, ALLOW, 0, 1, {arg=0, op=SCMP_CMP_EQ(4), datum_a=0, datum_b=0}) — read allowed only when fd==0
main() at 0x14fc: call rax executes user shellcode under the seccomp sandbox
Shellcode can call close(0) to free fd 0, then open('/flag') which reuses fd 0, then read(0,buf,n) reads file content, then write(1,buf,n) outputs to stdout

security_check.expected: The seccomp sandbox should prevent shellcode from reading arbitrary files and exfiltrating their contents. If read is restricted to fd==0 (stdin) and write to fd==1 (stdout), the sandbox should ensure that only stdin can be read and only stdout can be written to.
security_check.actual: The fd constraints (fd==0 for read, fd==1 for write) only check the integer fd value, not the underlying file object. Since close(0)+open() reassigns fd 0 to a new file, and close(1)+open() reassigns fd 1 to a new file, the constraints are bypassable via fd reuse.
security_check.missing_or_incorrect: The sandbox allows close(), open(), and openat() without any restrictions, enabling fd number reuse. The fd==0 and fd==1 constraints are not bound to the original stdin/stdout file objects — they are purely integer comparisons that can be defeated by reassigning fd numbers. A correct sandbox would either: (a) not allow open/openat at all, (b) use O_PATH or other mechanisms to prevent reading file contents, or (c) not allow close() on fd 0 and fd 1.

vulnerable_operation.operation: seccomp_rule_add with SCMP_CMP_EQ fd constraint combined with unrestricted close/open/openat
vulnerable_operation.expression: read(fd) allowed iff fd==0; write(fd) allowed iff fd==1; close(fd) always allowed; open() always allowed; openat() always allowed → close(0)+open(path) reuses fd 0 → read(0) reads from opened file
vulnerable_operation.target: seccomp BPF filter / file descriptor table

impact.reason: The seccomp sandbox's intended access control (restricting file read to stdin and file write to stdout) is bypassable. Shellcode can read arbitrary file contents by reusing fd 0 via close(0)+open(target_file), then read(0,buf,n). This bypasses the sandbox's file access restriction, achieving unauthorized file read. The file content can then be exfiltrated via write(1,buf,n) to stdout. Preconditions: (1) shellcode execution is reached (always true by design), (2) a target file path is known or guessable (e.g., /flag, ./flag), (3) the target file is readable by the process. Evidence is static (disassembly of seccomp rules).

evidence.description: Write rule struct setup: [rbp-0x30]=0 (arg=0), [rbp-0x2c]=4 (op=SCMP_CMP_EQ), [rbp-0x28]=1 (datum_a=1), [rbp-0x20]=0 (datum_b=0). seccomp_rule_add(ctx, 0x7fff0000, 1, 1, {arg=0, op=EQ, datum_a=1}) — write allowed only when fd==1.

Read rule struct setup: [rbp-0x50]=0 (arg=0), [rbp-0x4c]=4 (op=SCMP_CMP_EQ), [rbp-0x48]=0 (datum_a=0), [rbp-0x40]=0 (datum_b=0). seccomp_rule_add(ctx, 0x7fff0000, 0, 1, {arg=0, op=EQ, datum_a=0}) — read allowed only when fd==0.
open rule: seccomp_rule_add(ctx, 0x7fff0000, 2, 0) — open() allowed with NO argument constraints (arg_cnt=0). Any file can be opened.
openat rule: seccomp_rule_add(ctx, 0x7fff0000, 0x101, 0) — openat() allowed with NO argument constraints.
close rule: seccomp_rule_add(ctx, 0x7fff0000, 3, 0) — close() allowed with NO argument constraints. Any fd can be closed, including fd 0 and fd 1.

Combined effect of E001-E005: read restricted to fd==0, write restricted to fd==1, but close+open are unrestricted. Linux fd allocation assigns the lowest available fd number. close(0) frees fd 0; subsequent open(path) reuses fd 0 for the new file. read(0,buf,n) then reads from the opened file, not stdin. This bypasses the fd==0 constraint. The SCMP_CMP_EQ comparison checks only the integer fd value, not the file object identity.

seccomp_init(0) sets default action SCMP_ACT_KILL — all syscalls not explicitly whitelisted are killed. execve(59), execveat(322), mprotect(10), munmap(11), fork/clone, socket, stat/lstat, getdents, chdir, getcwd are all denied. This confirms the sandbox is intended to prevent code execution and network access, making the fd-reuse file read bypass the primary attack vector.

verification_required: Confirm the exact BPF filter generated by libseccomp 2.5.5 at runtime (S1 noted seccomp-tools not available; BPF dump via ptrace would confirm the SCMP_CMP_EQ constraints are correctly translated)
Confirm that close(0)+open('/flag') actually reuses fd 0 under the runtime environment (standard Linux behavior, but should be verified dynamically)
Determine the flag file path (not embedded in binary; common paths /flag, ./flag, /home/*/flag should be tested)
Verify that the read(0) constraint is truly fd==0 and not fd<=0 or fd<1 (SCMP_CMP_EQ=4 confirms exact equality, but runtime BPF dump would provide certainty)

non_vulnerabilities.description: mmap RWX page allocation and shellcode read/execute path
non_vulnerabilities.reason: mmap(0, 0x1000, 7, 0x22, -1, 0) allocates exactly 4096 bytes. read(0, buf, 0xfff) reads at most 4095 bytes into the 4096-byte page — no buffer overflow (read size 0xfff < page size 0x1000). mmap return value is checked against MAP_FAILED (-1) at 0x14be. read return value is checked for zero at 0x14eb. The integer arithmetic (0x1000 - 1 = 0xfff, movsxd sign-extension) is correct with no overflow. The call rax at 0x1500 is intentional shellcode execution by design.

_abort() calls printf('%s', msg) at 0x13e9 where msg is a constant string pointer ('mmap failed!' or 'read failed!') passed from main. The format string is a literal '%s' at 0x2008, and the user-controlled data is passed as the second argument (rsi), not as the format string. No format string vulnerability.

init() calls setvbuf(stdin/stdout/stderr, 0, 2, 0) for unbuffered I/O, alarm(60) for timeout, and setup_seccomp(). All calls use constant arguments. No user-controlled input reaches this function. No vulnerability.

non_vulnerabilities.description: Error accumulation in seccomp rule setup
non_vulnerabilities.reason: setup_seccomp() accumulates errors from seccomp_rule_add and seccomp_load return values via OR into [rbp-0xc], then checks if nonzero at 0x13b7 and calls exit(1). This error handling is correct — if any seccomp_rule_add or seccomp_load fails, the program exits. No vulnerability in the error handling logic itself (the vulnerability is in the rule configuration, not the error checking).

unresolved.description: S1 reported 11 seccomp rules including a 'redundant unconstrained read' rule (rule #6). Actual disassembly shows only 10 seccomp_rule_add calls. There is NO unconstrained read rule — read has exactly one rule with fd==0 constraint. S1's claim that 'read is fully allowed for any fd' is incorrect.
unresolved.reason: S1 may have miscounted or misidentified a rule. The disassembly clearly shows 10 seccomp_rule_add calls, and the read rule at 0x12ed has arg_cnt=1 with SCMP_CMP_EQ constraint on arg0==0.
unresolved.required_next_step: S3 should dump the actual BPF filter at runtime (via seccomp-tools or ptrace PTRACE_SECCOMP_GET_FILTER) to confirm the exact filter rules and resolve the discrepancy with S1's report.

unresolved.description: The exact flag file path is unknown — no file path string is embedded in the binary.
unresolved.reason: The binary contains no hardcoded flag path. The challenge likely expects shellcode to open a flag file at a common path (/flag, ./flag, etc.).
unresolved.required_next_step: S3/S4 should determine the flag file path through environment inspection or testing common paths.
